questions.title: RAII: Why C++ Ties Resource Lifetime to Scope
questions.prompt: Explain what RAII (Resource Acquisition Is Initialization) means in C++, and why it's the idiom nearly all modern C++ resource management is built on. Use an example other than a smart pointer -- a file handle or a network connection -- to show why it matters.
questions.modelAnswer: RAII ties the lifetime of a resource -- heap memory, a file handle, a socket, a lock -- to the lifetime of an object. The resource is acquired in the object's constructor and released in its destructor. Because C++ guarantees a stack object's destructor runs deterministically the moment it goes out of scope -- whether that's normal control flow, an early return, or an exception unwinding through the scope -- the resource is released no matter how the function exits. The programmer never has to remember to call a cleanup function on every exit path; the type system does it automatically. A FileHandle class that opens a file in its constructor and calls fclose in its destructor is a direct example: once an instance goes out of scope, the file closes, even if the function threw partway through. This is exactly the mechanism std::unique_ptr and std::lock_guard build on; they are just RAII applied to heap memory and mutexes respectively.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd describe RAII as 'the destructor is the cleanup code, and C++ guarantees it runs.' Instead of writing open() then remembering to close() on every single return path -- including the ones you forget about, like an exception -- you wrap the resource in a small class: acquire it in the constructor, release it in the destructor. The moment that object's scope ends, cleanup just happens, automatically, deterministically, no garbage collector involved. It's the single idea that makes modern C++ memory-safe-feeling without a GC -- unique_ptr, lock_guard, ifstream, they're all the same trick applied to a different resource.
commonMistakes: Thinking RAII only applies to smart pointers, not files, sockets, or locks
Thinking RAII only guards against exceptions, when it also protects every ordinary early return
Writing a class with acquire-in-constructor but a separate manual cleanup() method instead of putting release logic in the destructor, defeating the whole point
keyPoints: A resource is acquired in a constructor and released in the matching destructor
Destructor execution is deterministic and runs on every exit path, including exceptions
RAII removes the need to remember manual cleanup on each return path
Smart pointers, lock_guard, and file streams are all RAII applied to a specific resource

questions.title: Stack vs. Heap: Lifetime, Speed, and a Classic Bug
questions.prompt: What's the difference between stack and heap allocation in C++? Walk through why returning a pointer to a local (stack) variable from a function is a bug, and how you'd fix it.
questions.modelAnswer: Stack memory is allocated and freed automatically as functions are called and return -- every local variable lives in the current function's stack frame, and the whole frame is popped the instant the function returns, destroying those variables. It's extremely fast because there's no allocation bookkeeping, but strictly scoped: a stack object cannot outlive the block that created it. Heap memory, requested explicitly with new, has a lifetime completely independent of scope -- it lives until something explicitly calls delete on it, even long after the function that allocated it has returned. Returning a pointer to a local variable (e.g. `double* make_price() { double price = 182.35; return &price; }`) is a bug because the moment the function returns, that stack frame is popped and `price` ceases to exist; the returned pointer refers to memory that may already be reused by something else. Dereferencing it afterward is undefined behavior -- it might print a plausible-looking stale value, garbage, or crash, unpredictably. The fix is to return by value (the stack object is copied or moved out safely before the frame is popped) or allocate on the heap and return ownership through a smart pointer.
questions.professionalAnswer: Stack is the 'free, automatic, scoped' memory -- it's gone the second the function returns, no action needed from you. Heap is the 'you asked for it, you own it until you say otherwise' memory. The classic beginner bug is handing out the address of a stack variable and expecting it to still mean something after the function that owned it has already returned -- it's reading memory that's already been reclaimed. The fix is almost always to just return the value itself rather than a pointer to it; modern C++ makes that efficient via move semantics, so there's rarely a real reason to reach for a raw pointer here at all.
questions.example: double* p = make_price(); std::cout << *p; // undefined behavior -- price's stack frame is already gone
commonMistakes: Returning the address of a local variable instead of returning by value
Assuming a crash will happen immediately, when the bug can silently print a plausible stale value instead
Thinking heap memory is automatically freed the way stack memory is

Returning a pointer/reference to a local variable is undefined behavior once the frame is popped
Returning by value (relying on move semantics) is the safe, idiomatic fix

questions.title: Fix This Leak With a Smart Pointer
questions.prompt: The function below leaks memory on every call. Rewrite it using a smart pointer so the leak is structurally impossible, and explain why your version can't leak even if an exception is thrown partway through processing.
questions.modelAnswer: Replace the raw new/delete with std::unique_ptr (constructed via std::make_unique), and let the compiler-generated destructor handle cleanup. Because unique_ptr's destructor runs deterministically when it goes out of scope -- on a normal return, an early return, or an exception propagating through -- the Order it owns is always deleted exactly once, with no code path left that forgets to call delete. There's also no way to accidentally double-delete or delete twice, since unique_ptr can't be copied, only moved, so at most one owner ever exists.
questions.professionalAnswer: The fix is almost mechanical once you see it: swap `Order* o = new Order(...)` for `auto o = std::make_unique<Order>(...)`, drop the manual delete entirely, and use `o->` exactly as before. The reason it can't leak on an exception is the same reason RAII works everywhere -- the unique_ptr is a stack object, and stack objects get their destructors run during exception unwinding, same as a normal return. You genuinely don't have to think about the exception path separately; it's handled by the same mechanism as the happy path.
commonMistakes: Forgetting std::make_unique and still writing new T(...) manually, which loses the exception-safety benefit make_unique provides during argument evaluation
Manually calling delete on the pointer the unique_ptr owns, causing a double-free
Using std::shared_ptr by habit when exclusive ownership (unique_ptr) is all that's needed, adding unnecessary reference-counting overhead
keyPoints: std::unique_ptr's destructor automatically deletes the owned object

unique_ptr cannot be copied, only moved, preventing double ownership

questions.title: Why Returning a Large Vector by Value Is Cheap in Modern C++
questions.prompt: Write a function that builds a std::vector<double> of a million simulated prices and returns it by value. Explain why this doesn't copy a million doubles in modern C++, and what would have happened in C++03.
questions.modelAnswer: Because the vector being returned is a local variable about to go out of scope, it's treated as an rvalue at the return statement, and the compiler either elides the copy entirely or invokes std::vector's move constructor -- which just swaps a few internal pointers (data, size, capacity) between the local vector and the caller's destination, with zero element-by-element copying. In C++03, before move semantics existed, the same code would have performed a full copy: allocate a new million-element buffer and copy every double into it, then destroy the original -- a real, measurable cost for something that's conceptually just handing the data to the caller. This is exactly why modern C++ guidance is to write the natural return-by-value signature rather than an output parameter or raw pointer 'to avoid a copy' the old C++03 way demanded.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd just write the obvious signature -- build the vector locally, return it by value -- and trust the compiler. That used to be bad advice in C++03, where it really did copy the whole buffer, which is why you see a lot of old code passing an output reference parameter instead. Move semantics changed that: the compiler sees you're returning a local that's about to die anyway, so it moves the internal buffer pointer instead of copying every element. It's one of the clearest cases where modern C++ let people go back to writing readable code without paying a performance tax for it.
commonMistakes: Still writing an output-parameter style signature (passing a vector& to fill) out of old C++03 habit when return-by-value is now equally fast
Thinking std::move is required on the return statement -- it isn't; the compiler already treats the return of a local as a move candidate
Assuming the one-million-element copy still happens and adding unnecessary manual optimization

std::vector's move constructor transfers internal pointers, not elements

Modern guidance favors natural return-by-value signatures over output parameters

questions.title: Diagnosing a Memory Leak With AddressSanitizer
questions.prompt: A pricing service's memory usage grows steadily over days of continuous operation and is eventually killed by the OS. You suspect a leak. Walk through how you would confirm it and locate the exact allocation site using AddressSanitizer.
questions.modelAnswer: First, I'd reproduce the behavior under a controlled, repeatable load rather than waiting days in production -- run the service's normal request path in a loop long enough that a leak's growth becomes visible. I'd rebuild the binary with -fsanitize=address -g (ASan plus debug symbols) and run that instrumented build against the same load. ASan tracks every allocation and, on program exit (or via a periodic leak check if the binary runs continuously), reports exactly which allocations were never freed, along with the full call stack of where each one was allocated. That report points directly at the offending new/malloc call, rather than at the symptom of rising memory, which is the key advantage over just watching OS-level memory metrics. Once the leak is isolated to a specific allocation site, the fix is usually either a missing delete on an exception path, a container that keeps growing (e.g. a cache with no eviction), or a raw pointer where a smart pointer should own the object.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't try to find this by staring at production memory graphs -- that only tells you memory is growing, not where. I'd get a build with ASan turned on, hammer it with the same traffic pattern that triggers the growth, and let ASan's leak report do the work: it gives you the exact call stack of the allocation that never got freed. In my experience the usual suspects are an exception path that skips a cleanup step, or a cache/map that accumulates entries nobody ever removes -- ASan tells you which of those it actually is instead of making you guess.
commonMistakes: Trying to find the leak by reading code by eye instead of using a tool built for exactly this
Running ASan once with light load and concluding there's no leak when the leak only shows up at sustained volume
Confusing steadily rising memory with a one-time startup allocation, instead of confirming it keeps growing under sustained load
keyPoints: Reproduce the leak under controlled, repeatable load rather than relying on production
Compile with -fsanitize=address -g to get instrumented, line-accurate reports
ASan's leak report gives the full allocation call stack, not just a memory-growth symptom

questions.title: What an Order Management System (OMS) Layer Is For
questions.prompt: A junior developer asks why the strategy code calls an internal `OrderManager.submit(order)` instead of talking to the broker's REST API directly. How would you explain the purpose of an OMS abstraction layer?
questions.modelAnswer: An OMS layer is the stable internal interface the strategy code calls -- submit an order, cancel an order, query status -- that then translates those calls into whatever protocol the specific broker actually speaks underneath, whether that's a REST API, the FIX protocol, or a vendor's native SDK. The strategy's signal, sizing, and risk logic shouldn't need to know or care which protocol is underneath; it just calls a stable method. This matters for a few concrete reasons: if the firm adds a second broker or the first broker changes its API, only the OMS layer's implementation changes, not every strategy that submits orders. It's also the natural place to put cross-cutting concerns that every order needs regardless of broker -- generating a unique client order ID for idempotent retries, tracking the order lifecycle (new, working, partially filled, filled, rejected), and applying pre-trade risk checks -- once, rather than duplicated inside every strategy.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd tell them: imagine we add a second broker next quarter, or the first one changes their API -- without an OMS layer, every single strategy that calls the broker directly has to be touched. With the OMS in between, only one piece of code changes. It's also just a cleaner separation of concerns: the strategy's job is deciding what to trade, not managing retries, client order IDs, or parsing a specific broker's JSON response format. We want that logic written and tested once, not copy-pasted into every strategy that happens to trade.
commonMistakes: Thinking the OMS layer is only about code reuse, missing that it also centralizes correctness-critical logic like idempotent retries
Letting strategy code reach around the OMS to call the broker directly for a 'quick' feature, which defeats the abstraction over time
Assuming one broker's API will never change or that a second broker will never be added

Centralizes cross-cutting correctness logic: client order IDs, order lifecycle, risk checks
Isolates the impact of adding a broker or a broker API change to one place

questions.title: Tell Me About Yourself (Quant Developer Recruiter Screen)
questions.prompt: Walk me through your background and why you're interested in a quantitative developer role here.
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer for a quant-developer-track recruiter screen stays under 90 seconds and moves through three parts: background (what you've built and in what language/domain -- emphasize systems and performance work, not just research), one concrete project that demonstrates production-engineering judgment (e.g. a C++ pricing library exposed to Python, or a backtest engine you hardened for realistic execution), stated in one or two sentences including a real result, and what you're looking for (a role where correctness and latency both matter, ideally naming something specific about the firm's stack or desk). questions.title: Knowing Which Interview You're In: Python Round vs. C++ Round
questions.prompt: How do you figure out whether a quant developer interview is going to test Python, C++, or both -- and how would you prepare differently for each?
questions.modelAnswer: The honest answer is the job posting and the role itself are the first signal: research-flavored roles at systematic funds tend to test Python, specifically pandas/NumPy fluency, because that's the actual daily tool; latency-sensitive roles -- market making, HFT infrastructure, low-latency trading systems -- test C++, because execution speed in production is the entire point of the job. Many postings test both at different stages of the loop. If the posting doesn't make it clear, the right move is to ask the recruiter directly during the screen which language the technical rounds will use -- that's a completely normal, expected question, not a sign of being under-prepared. Preparation differs accordingly: for a Python round, practice vectorized pandas/NumPy problems and be ready to explain why vectorization is fast, not just that it is; for a C++ round, be fluent in pointers vs. references, stack vs. heap, RAII, and comfortable with a focused problem set that exercises memory management directly, like implementing a small fixed-size ring buffer, not just abstract algorithm puzzles.
questions.professionalAnswer: I just ask. Recruiters get this question all the time and it's a completely reasonable thing to want to know before you spend a weekend prepping the wrong thing. If it's a systematic-fund research role, I lean into pandas/NumPy fluency and make sure I can explain why vectorized code is actually fast under the hood. If it's a market-making or infra-heavy role, I make sure pointers vs. references, stack vs. heap, and RAII are second nature, and I practice a couple of small memory-management exercises -- something like a ring buffer -- rather than only leetcode-style puzzles, because that's closer to what they'll actually probe.

questions.title: Pointer, Reference, or Value: The Decision Rule
questions.prompt: A teammate passes every function argument by raw pointer 'just in case the object doesn't exist.' Walk through the actual decision rule for choosing between pass-by-value, pass-by-const-reference, pass-by-reference, and pass-by-pointer, and say when a pointer is actually the right call.
questions.modelAnswer: The decision comes down to size, mutability, and whether 'no object at all' is a real, meaningful possibility. Pass small, cheap types (int, double, bool) by value -- copying them costs nothing and avoids any indirection. Pass anything larger (a struct, a std::string, a std::vector) by const reference when the function only needs to read it and the argument is guaranteed to exist -- this avoids a copy while promising the caller their data won't be modified. Pass by plain reference (no const) specifically when the function needs to modify the caller's object in place, and that object is guaranteed to exist. Reserve a raw pointer (or better, a smart pointer or std::optional) for the one case none of the others handle: when the argument might legitimately be absent -- nullptr is a real, valid state the function needs to check for. Defaulting to pointers everywhere throws away the compiler's guarantee that a reference is never null, and forces every caller to think about null-checking even when 'no object' was never actually a real possibility for that parameter.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd walk through it as a short checklist: is it small and cheap -- pass by value. Is it bigger but read-only and will definitely exist -- const reference. Does the function need to change it in place and it'll definitely exist -- plain reference. Only reach for a pointer (or std::optional) when 'this might not exist' is a real case the function has to handle, not a hypothetical. Pointers everywhere isn't 'safer,' it's actually less safe -- a reference can't be null, so using one wherever possible removes an entire category of bug the 'just in case' pointer habit reintroduces for no reason.

Passing a large struct or std::string by value out of habit, causing an unnecessary copy
Using a non-const reference for a parameter the function never actually modifies

questions.title: Why C++ Still Wins the Latency Argument
questions.prompt: A new grad asks why a pricing library would ever be written in C++ instead of Python, when Python is so much faster to develop in. What's the actual technical answer, beyond 'it's faster'?
questions.modelAnswer: The real answer isn't just raw speed, it's predictable, worst-case control. Python and Java run on a managed heap with a garbage collector that reclaims memory on its own schedule, not the program's -- which means it can pause execution at a moment the program doesn't control, and that pause is unacceptable for code that must react to a market-data tick in a few hundred nanoseconds. C++ has no garbage collector: every object's lifetime is determined entirely by the code you write, through RAII and scope, so there's no hidden pause waiting to happen. On top of that, C++ compiles straight to machine code with no interpreter or virtual machine layer in between, and its guiding design goal of 'zero-overhead abstraction' means you can write expressive, high-level code (classes, templates, the STL) without paying a runtime penalty for it. That combination -- no GC pauses, no interpreter, abstractions that cost nothing -- is why exchange matching engines, pricing libraries, and execution systems are written in C++ even though Python is genuinely faster to develop in for research.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd say it's not about Python being slow on average, it's about worst-case behavior. A garbage collector can decide to pause your program at the worst possible moment, and in a system reacting to live prices, that pause is the whole ballgame. C++ gives you full control over memory and execution with no such surprise, and it does that without forcing you to write ugly, low-level code -- that's the 'zero-overhead abstraction' idea. That's why the pattern across the industry is: research happens in Python because it's fast to write, and the pieces that actually have to react in real time get written or rewritten in C++.

questions.title: double vs. float, and Why You Never Compare Prices With ==
questions.prompt: Explain why financial code should default to double over float, why a plain int can silently overflow when counting something like nanosecond timestamps, and why you should never compare two computed prices with ==.
questions.modelAnswer: double is a 64-bit floating-point type with roughly twice the precision of float's 32 bits, and in financial calculations that extra precision matters because rounding error compounds across millions of arithmetic operations -- a price computed through a long chain of multiplications and divisions in float will have accumulated visibly more error than the same chain in double. Integer overflow is a separate but related trap: a plain int is commonly only 32 bits, so counting something that can genuinely grow large -- nanosecond timestamps, cumulative share counts -- in a plain int can silently wrap around to a nonsensical value with no warning or crash, rather than failing loudly; the fix is a wider type like long long or a fixed-width int64_t. Comparing two floating-point values with == is unreliable because two numbers that are mathematically equal can differ in their last bit or two due to how floating-point arithmetic rounds intermediate results -- two prices computed through slightly different, but mathematically equivalent, code paths can fail an == check despite being 'the same' for any practical purpose. The fix is comparing against a small tolerance, such as std::abs(a - b) < 1e-9, rather than exact equality.
questions.professionalAnswer: Three separate habits, all for similar reasons: default to double for anything financial, because the extra precision avoids visibly worse rounding drift over long chains of math. Watch integer sizes -- a plain int silently overflowing on a large share count or a nanosecond timestamp is a real, quiet bug, not a theoretical one, so reach for long long or int64_t once the range matters. And never write if (priceA == priceB) for computed floating-point values -- floating-point arithmetic just doesn't guarantee bit-for-bit equality across different but equivalent calculations, so I always compare against a small tolerance instead.

if (std::abs(priceA - priceB) < 1e-9) { /* treat as equal */ }
// not: if (priceA == priceB)

questions.title: Pass by Value vs. const Reference: The Single Highest-Impact Habit
questions.prompt: An Order struct has an int id, a double price, a long quantity, and a std::string symbol. Why does a function signature like void log_order(Order o) cost more than it looks like, and what's the fix?
questions.modelAnswer: void log_order(Order o) passes the Order by value, which means every single call copies the entire struct -- including a deep copy of the std::string symbol's heap-allocated character data, not just a shallow bit-copy. For a function called on every order in a hot path, that's a real, entirely avoidable cost, and it's easy to miss because the signature looks completely ordinary. The fix is void log_order(const Order& o): a reference parameter doesn't create a new object at all, it's just another name for the caller's existing Order, so no copy happens, and const documents (and the compiler enforces) that the function won't modify the caller's data. The rule of thumb that covers this and nearly every similar case: pass small, cheap types (int, double, bool) by value, and pass anything larger -- structs, classes, std::string, std::vector -- by const reference unless the function specifically needs to modify the caller's object.
questions.professionalAnswer: This is one of those bugs that doesn't look like a bug at all -- the signature reads perfectly naturally. The problem is purely that passing Order by value silently copies the whole thing, string data included, on every single call. Changing the parameter to const Order& fixes it with essentially no downside: no copy, and const makes the compiler enforce that the function can't mutate the caller's order. I treat this as close to a default habit now -- value for small primitive types, const reference for anything bigger that's read-only -- and it eliminates most of the unnecessary copying you'd otherwise find scattered through a codebase.

questions.title: struct vs. class: The One Real Difference
questions.prompt: A teammate insists struct and class are fundamentally different features in C++. Are they? Explain the actual distinction, and why a Position type that enforces 'quantity and average price can never drift out of sync' should be a class with private data, not a public struct.
questions.modelAnswer: struct and class are the same language feature in C++, with exactly one difference: members of a struct are public by default, members of a class are private by default -- that's the entire distinction, nothing more. Convention uses struct for simple, passive data bags where every field is meant to be freely read and written, and class for types that own behavior and need to enforce rules about their own data. A Position holding a quantity and an average price is exactly the second case: if both fields are public, any piece of calling code can set quantity without touching avgPrice, letting the two drift out of sync with no way to prevent it. Making them private and exposing only a method like addFill(fillQty, fillPrice) that updates both together, consistently, means that method is the only path into the object's state -- the invariant 'quantity and avgPrice agree with each other' can never be violated from outside the class, because outside code has no way to touch either field directly.
questions.professionalAnswer: They're the same thing under the hood -- the only actual difference is the default access level, public for struct, private for class. The reason it matters for something like Position isn't the keyword, it's the design decision it signals: if quantity and avgPrice are public, two unrelated pieces of calling code can update one without the other and quietly corrupt the object's own internal consistency. Making them private and only exposing a method like addFill() that updates both together is what actually prevents that -- the class keyword is just a default that nudges you toward the right habit, not a different mechanism from struct.
commonMistakes: Believing struct and class are different mechanisms rather than differing only in default access

questions.title: Why price() Needs to Be virtual
questions.prompt: A Future and an Option both derive from an abstract Instrument base class with a price() method. A junior developer removes the virtual keyword from Instrument::price() because 'it compiles fine without it.' What breaks, and why does it compile without any error or warning?
questions.modelAnswer: Without virtual, calling price() through a base-class pointer or reference always calls Instrument::price() specifically, regardless of what the actual underlying object is -- this is called static (compile-time) dispatch, and the compiler resolves it purely from the pointer's declared type, not the object's real type. It compiles fine because that's completely legal C++; the compiler has no way to know this isn't what you wanted, since removing virtual doesn't create any error, it just changes which function gets called. The practical break shows up the moment code iterates a std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Instrument>> containing both Futures and Options and calls instr->price() on each -- every single call would silently return Instrument's own (likely wrong, possibly non-existent without a body) price() instead of each object's actual derived pricing logic. With virtual, the same call performs dynamic dispatch: at runtime, the call looks up the actual object's real type and calls that type's override -- which is the entire point of writing a polymorphic instrument book in the first place.
questions.professionalAnswer: The dangerous part is exactly that it compiles cleanly -- there's no error, no warning, just quietly wrong behavior. Without virtual, a call through an Instrument* always resolves to Instrument::price() at compile time, based on the pointer's declared type, not what it actually points to. The bug becomes real the moment you loop over a mixed vector of Futures and Options through base pointers and call price() on each -- every single one calls the base version instead of its own, and nothing about that looks broken until you look at the actual numbers coming out. virtual is what makes the call look up the real object's type at runtime instead -- it's not a performance nicety, it's the entire mechanism that makes polymorphism work at all.

questions.title: vector, map, or unordered_map: A Quick Decision Guide
questions.prompt: You need to store last-traded prices keyed by ticker symbol, and you'll look them up constantly but never need them in any particular order. Which STL container fits, and how would your answer change if you did need them iterated in sorted symbol order?

questions.title: Capture by Value vs. by Reference in a Lambda
questions.prompt: Explain the difference between [threshold](double price) {...} and [&threshold](double price) {...}, and give a concrete scenario where using the wrong one produces a bug that's easy to miss.
questions.modelAnswer: [threshold] captures threshold by value -- the lambda stores its own independent copy, frozen at the moment the lambda is created, and later changes to the outer threshold variable have no effect on what the lambda sees. [&threshold] captures it by reference -- the lambda holds onto the actual outer variable, so if threshold changes after the lambda was created but before it's called, the lambda will see the new value. The bug scenario: if you build a filtering lambda with [&threshold] inside a loop that also modifies threshold on each iteration, and then store that lambda to call later, every stored lambda ends up referencing the same outer threshold variable -- by the time any of them actually run, they'll all see whatever threshold's final value happened to be, not the value that was 'current' when each lambda was created. Capturing by value instead ([threshold]) freezes each lambda's own copy at creation time, giving each one the value you actually intended it to have.
questions.professionalAnswer: Capture by value takes a snapshot right then; capture by reference keeps a live link to the actual outer variable. The bug I'd watch for is building a bunch of lambdas in a loop, capturing a loop variable by reference, and only calling those lambdas later -- by then the outer variable has already changed, often to its final value, so every lambda sees the same wrong thing instead of the value it had when it was created. My default is to capture by value unless I specifically need the lambda to see live changes to that variable -- naming the capture explicitly (`[threshold]` rather than a blanket `[=]`) also documents exactly what the lambda depends on.

questions.title: Compiler, Linker, and Build System: Three Different Jobs
questions.prompt: A teammate says 'the compiler is broken' when their multi-file project fails with an undefined reference error after g++ runs successfully on each file. What's actually going on, and why is this a linker problem, not a compiler problem?
questions.modelAnswer: The compiler (g++, clang++) and the linker solve different problems, and conflating them is exactly what causes this confusion. The compiler only ever looks at one .cpp file (one translation unit) at a time, translating it into an object file -- if each file compiles without error, the compiler did its job correctly and completely. The linker's separate job is to combine multiple object files into one executable, resolving every function call in one file to its actual definition, wherever that definition lives. 'Undefined reference' is specifically a linker error: it means the linker found a call to some function but never found that function's definition in any of the object files it was given to link -- usually because a .cpp file containing the definition was never compiled and included in the link step, or the function's signature doesn't exactly match between its declaration and its definition. The compiler isn't broken at all; it did exactly what it was asked to do on each file individually. The fix is almost always making sure every .cpp file that defines something the program calls is actually being compiled and passed to the final link command.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd clarify the split first: the compiler translates one file at a time and has no idea what's in any other file; the linker is the one that stitches multiple files' object code together afterward. 'Undefined reference' is the linker telling you it found a call to something but never found where that something is actually defined -- almost always because a .cpp file with the definition wasn't compiled and handed to the final link step, or the declaration and definition don't quite match. Nothing about that means the compiler failed; each file compiled exactly fine on its own, which is the whole clue that this is a linking problem, not a compilation one.

questions.title: const double* vs. double* const: Fix the Declaration
questions.prompt: A function needs a pointer that can be repointed to different prices over time, but every price it points to must never be modified through that pointer. Which of const double* p and double* const p is correct, and why does the other one fail to express the requirement?

Mixing these two up is one of the most common const-correctness mistakes in C++, and reading right-to-left from the star is the trick that makes it unambiguous every time.

questions.prompt: Your build fails with: undefined reference to `price_option(double, double)'. The function is declared in pricer.h and defined in pricer.cpp, and main.cpp includes pricer.h and calls it. Walk through how you'd track down the actual cause.
questions.modelAnswer: This is a linker error, meaning the linker found a call to price_option but never found a matching definition among the object files it was given. The first thing to check is whether pricer.cpp was actually compiled and included in the final link command at all -- it's extremely common to add a new .cpp file to a project and forget to add it to the build command or CMakeLists.txt, in which case its definitions simply never get compiled into any object file the linker sees. If pricer.cpp is being compiled, the next check is whether the function's signature in the header exactly matches the one in the .cpp file -- a mismatch in parameter types, constness, or even just one being in a namespace and the other not, produces a different mangled symbol name, which the linker will treat as two entirely unrelated functions, with one of them (the declaration-only one being called) never actually defined anywhere as far as the linker can tell.
questions.professionalAnswer: First thing I check: is pricer.cpp actually part of the build? It's an easy thing to forget when adding a new file -- the header's included everywhere, but nobody added the .cpp to the compile/link step, so the function was declared but never actually compiled into any object file. If it is being compiled, I'd check the exact signature matches between the header's declaration and the .cpp's definition -- parameter types, const-ness, namespace -- because even a small mismatch produces a different linker symbol, and the linker sees that as a totally different, never-defined function rather than giving you a helpful 'these don't match' message.
commonMistakes: Assuming the header's declaration alone is enough, forgetting the .cpp file must also be compiled and linked
Not checking for an exact signature match between the declaration and definition
Treating this as a compiler problem rather than recognizing it's specifically a linker-stage error

Check first whether the .cpp file with the definition is actually part of the build/link step
Check for an exact signature match between the header declaration and the .cpp definition
A signature mismatch produces a different linker symbol, which looks like a missing definition

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly frames this as a linker-stage problem
Checks whether the defining .cpp file is actually compiled/linked
Checks for a signature mismatch between declaration and definition

questions.title: Debugging a Silent Out-of-Bounds Vector Access
questions.prompt: A pricing function reads prices[prices.size()] somewhere deep in a loop and sometimes produces a plausible-looking but wrong number, with no crash and no error. Explain why this doesn't crash, and how you'd actually catch it.
questions.modelAnswer: prices[prices.size()] is reading one past the last valid element -- operator[] on std::vector performs no bounds checking at all, so this is undefined behavior, not a guaranteed error. In practice, that often means reading whatever happens to sit in memory immediately after the vector's allocated buffer, which can be leftover data from an earlier allocation, part of the vector's own internal bookkeeping, or genuinely unmapped memory. Because it's frequently 'just some other number already in memory' rather than unmapped memory, it often doesn't crash at all -- it silently returns a plausible-looking garbage value, which is exactly what makes this bug dangerous: nothing about the program's behavior announces that anything went wrong. The right way to actually catch this is to compile with AddressSanitizer (-fsanitize=address), which instruments every memory access and will flag this specific out-of-bounds read immediately, with the exact line number, the moment it happens during a test run -- rather than relying on the bug to eventually crash on its own, which it may never reliably do. A simpler, narrower fix for day-to-day safety is to use .at(i) instead of operator[] during development and testing, since .at() does bounds-check and throws an exception on an out-of-range index.
questions.professionalAnswer: The reason it doesn't crash is that operator[] on vector has no bounds checking at all -- reading one past the end is undefined behavior, and undefined behavior often just means 'reads whatever garbage happens to be in memory there,' which can look like a perfectly plausible number. That's what makes it genuinely dangerous rather than just broken. I wouldn't try to catch this by staring at the loop -- I'd rebuild with AddressSanitizer and run the same workload; ASan instruments every memory access and will flag this out-of-bounds read the instant it happens, with the exact line. For day-to-day safety during development, swapping operator[] for .at() also catches it immediately, since .at() bounds-checks and throws.
commonMistakes: Assuming any memory bug will reliably crash, rather than understanding undefined behavior can silently produce plausible garbage
Trying to spot an off-by-one index bug by code review alone instead of using a tool designed for exactly this
Not knowing that .at() bounds-checks while operator[] does not
keyPoints: std::vector::operator[] performs no bounds checking; an out-of-range access is undefined behavior
Undefined behavior can silently return plausible-looking garbage instead of crashing
AddressSanitizer (-fsanitize=address) catches out-of-bounds accesses immediately, with the exact location
.at() bounds-checks and throws, unlike operator[]

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains why operator[] out-of-bounds is undefined behavior without a bounds check
Explains why this often doesn't crash, just silently returns garbage
Names AddressSanitizer as the correct detection tool
Clarity

questions.title: Diagnosing an Object Slicing Bug
questions.prompt: A function takes an Instrument (by value, not by reference or pointer) and is supposed to work polymorphically across Future and Option. Instead, it always behaves like a plain Instrument no matter what's actually passed in. What's going wrong?
questions.modelAnswer: This is object slicing: a function parameter of type Instrument (by value) can only ever hold exactly an Instrument-sized object, so when a Future or Option is passed in, only its Instrument base-class portion gets copied into the parameter -- every derived-class member and the information about which derived type it actually was gets 'sliced off' and discarded. The parameter inside the function is now a genuine, plain Instrument object, not a Future or Option wearing an Instrument hat, so any virtual function call on it correctly (from the compiler's point of view) dispatches to Instrument's own version, because that's truly all that's left. This is completely different from the earlier virtual-dispatch bug, where the object itself was still the right type and only the pointer's static type caused wrong dispatch; here the actual object has been destroyed and replaced by a smaller copy. The fix is to never take a polymorphic base type by value -- take it by reference (const Instrument&) or by pointer/smart pointer (std::unique_ptr<Instrument> or Instrument*), both of which preserve the object's real, full type and let virtual dispatch work correctly.
questions.professionalAnswer: That's slicing, not a dispatch bug -- a real, structural difference from the 'forgot virtual' bug. Taking an Instrument by value means the function parameter can literally only ever be Instrument-sized; whatever extra data and type information a Future or Option carried gets thrown away during the copy, and what's left really is just a plain Instrument. Calling a virtual function on it is correctly calling Instrument's version, because by that point there's genuinely nothing else left to call. The fix is to never take a polymorphic type by value -- pass it by reference or pointer instead, so the real object (and its real type) stays intact.
commonMistakes: Confusing object slicing with a missing-virtual dispatch bug -- they look similar but have different root causes
Trying to fix it by adding virtual somewhere, when the object itself has already been destroyed by the copy
Not recognizing that pass-by-value is the root cause for any polymorphic base type
keyPoints: Passing a polymorphic base type by value copies only the base-class portion, discarding derived data and type
The resulting object genuinely is just the base type -- virtual dispatch is correctly calling the base version
This differs from a missing-virtual bug: here the object itself has been destroyed by the copy
The fix is passing by reference or pointer/smart pointer, never by value, for a polymorphic base type

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies this as object slicing
Correctly explains why the base-class portion alone is copied
Distinguishes this from a missing-virtual dispatch bug
Provides the correct fix (reference or pointer)

questions.title: Diagnosing a Bug From an Uninitialized Variable
questions.prompt: A function computes a running total that starts with a seemingly random, nonsensical value on some runs but not others, even though the input data looks identical. What's the likely cause, and how would you confirm it?
questions.modelAnswer: A local variable declared without an initializer (double total; with no = 0.0) has an indeterminate value -- it holds whatever bits happened to already be sitting in that stack memory from whatever used it previously, which is why the symptom is run-dependent rather than consistently wrong: different programs, different call histories, or even a different build can leave different leftover bits there. The fix is simply always initializing variables at declaration (double total = 0.0;), which removes the ambiguity entirely. To confirm this is actually the cause rather than guessing, compiling with -Wall -Wextra will often flag an obviously uninitialized read with a warning, and a tool like MemorySanitizer (or, more commonly available, simply running the suspect code path under a debugger and inspecting the variable's value right after declaration, before it's ever assigned) can confirm the exact uninitialized read directly.
questions.professionalAnswer: This smells like an uninitialized variable -- something like double total; with no = 0.0, which means it starts out holding whatever bits were already sitting in that stack slot from something else, not a clean zero. That's exactly why it's inconsistent between runs: different leftover memory contents each time. The fix is just always initializing at declaration. To actually confirm it rather than guess, -Wall -Wextra often catches an obviously uninitialized read as a warning, and worst case I'd step through in a debugger and look at the variable's value the moment it's declared, before any assignment happens.
commonMistakes: Assuming identical input data guarantees identical behavior, missing that uninitialized memory content varies run to run
Not compiling with -Wall -Wextra, which often flags an obviously uninitialized read directly
'Fixing' the symptom by resetting the variable somewhere later instead of initializing it at declaration
keyPoints: An uninitialized local variable holds an indeterminate value from leftover stack memory
This explains run-dependent, seemingly random behavior with identical input data
The fix is always initializing variables at declaration
Compiler warnings (-Wall -Wextra) or a debugger can confirm the uninitialized read

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies an uninitialized variable as the likely cause
Correctly explains why the symptom varies between runs
Describes a concrete way to confirm the diagnosis

questions.title: Debugging a Build That Behaves Differently Than Expected
questions.prompt: A teammate reports their pricing code is 'working fine' in testing but behaves strangely slow, and when you check their build command, there's no -O flag at all. Why would that alone explain sluggish behavior, and what's the risk of just adding -O3 blindly?
questions.modelAnswer: With no -O flag, the compiler defaults to -O0 -- essentially no optimization at all, which is exactly what you want for stepping through code in a debugger line by line, but it's dramatically slower than necessary for anything performance-sensitive, since none of the usual optimizations (inlining, loop unrolling, dead-code elimination) are applied. That alone, with zero logic changes, fully explains 'correct but sluggish' behavior -- the code was never actually measuring anything close to real performance. The fix for a release/performance build is -O2, the typical default optimization level that captures most of the safe, beneficial transformations. Blindly jumping straight to -O3 instead of -O2 is its own small risk: -O3 enables more aggressive transformations that occasionally make no difference or, less commonly, even regress performance on certain code, so the professional habit is to measure -O2 against -O3 on the actual workload rather than assuming more aggressive is automatically faster.
questions.professionalAnswer: No -O flag means -O0 by default -- debug-level, essentially unoptimized, which is perfect for stepping through in a debugger and genuinely bad for anything you care about the speed of. That alone, with no code changes, fully explains 'correct but slow.' I'd set -O2 as the release build's standard optimization level. I wouldn't reach straight for -O3 assuming it's automatically better, though -- the more aggressive transformations in -O3 sometimes don't help, or occasionally even hurt, depending on the code, so I'd actually measure -O2 against -O3 on the real workload rather than assuming.
commonMistakes: Not realizing the default build (no -O flag) is essentially unoptimized
Assuming -O3 is always strictly faster than -O2 without measuring
Treating a slow debug build as a logic bug instead of checking the build flags first
keyPoints: No -O flag defaults to -O0, essentially unoptimized, appropriate for debugging, not performance
-O2 is the typical release-build default, enabling most safe, beneficial optimizations
-O3 enables more aggressive transformations that should be measured, not assumed to always win
This class of 'slow' is purely a build-configuration issue, not a logic bug

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies the missing -O flag (defaulting to -O0) as the cause
Recommends -O2 as the appropriate release-build fix
Correctly cautions against assuming -O3 is automatically better

questions.title: Debugging an Infinite Loop From a Signed/Unsigned Comparison
questions.prompt: This loop is supposed to count down and stop, but it never terminates: for (int i = 10; i >= 0; --i) looks fine, but a similar loop using std::size_t instead of int hangs forever. Explain exactly why, using a loop counting down from a vector's size.
questions.modelAnswer: std::size_t (the type returned by .size()) is unsigned, meaning it can never represent a negative number -- it has no sign bit to hold one. A loop like for (std::size_t i = prices.size() - 1; i >= 0; --i) looks like it should stop once i reaches 0, but the moment --i is applied when i is already 0, it doesn't become -1; it wraps around to the maximum representable value for std::size_t (an enormous positive number, since unsigned arithmetic is defined to wrap modulo 2^N rather than go negative), and the condition i >= 0 is then still true -- in fact it's always true for an unsigned type, since an unsigned value can never be negative in the first place. The loop effectively never terminates in any reasonable time. The fix is either to use a signed integer type for a counter that needs to go negative or reach a sentinel below zero, or restructure the loop to avoid ever needing to compare an unsigned value against a condition that assumes negative values are reachable -- for example counting up through an offset instead of counting down to -1.
questions.professionalAnswer: The core fact is that std::size_t is unsigned, so it literally cannot represent -1 -- decrementing past zero wraps around to a huge positive number instead of going negative. That means i >= 0 is true for every single value an unsigned type can ever hold, so the loop condition never fails and it just runs forever (well past any reasonable time). I'd fix it either by using a signed type for a counter that's genuinely meant to reach negative values, or by rewriting the loop to count upward through an offset instead of counting down through zero with an unsigned type.
commonMistakes: Assuming decrementing an unsigned value below zero produces a negative number like a signed type would
Not recognizing i >= 0 is always true for any unsigned type, making the loop condition meaningless
Mixing signed and unsigned types in a comparison without considering the implicit conversion rules involved
keyPoints: std::size_t is unsigned and cannot represent negative values
Decrementing an unsigned value past zero wraps around to a very large positive number
i >= 0 is always true for an unsigned type, making that loop condition meaningless
Fix with a signed counter type, or restructure the loop to avoid comparing against an unreachable negative bound

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains that std::size_t is unsigned and cannot go negative
Correctly explains the wraparound behavior on decrement past zero
Explains why the loop condition is then always true
Provides a correct fix

questions.title: Debugging a Crash Caused by a Bad Sort Comparator
questions.prompt: A call to std::sort with a custom lambda comparator sometimes crashes or produces a corrupted-looking result, but only on certain input vectors. The comparator is [](double a, double b) { return a >= b; }. What's wrong with it?
questions.modelAnswer: A valid comparator for std::sort must implement strict weak ordering, which specifically requires that comp(x, x) is always false -- an element can never be considered to come strictly before itself. [](double a, double b) { return a >= b; } violates this: when a and b are equal (including when they're literally the same element being compared to itself during the algorithm's internal operations), it returns true, claiming the element comes before itself. std::sort's internal implementation relies on strict weak ordering holding to guarantee correct, bounded behavior; violating it is undefined behavior, which can manifest as anything from a subtly wrong sort order to memory corruption or a crash, and -- consistent with undefined behavior generally -- it often only shows up on certain input data (specifically, data containing duplicate or equal values) rather than failing consistently on every input. The fix is simply changing >= to >, which correctly returns false when a and b are equal.
questions.professionalAnswer: The bug is that >= breaks strict weak ordering, which std::sort's comparator is required to satisfy -- specifically, comparing an element to an equal value (including itself) must return false, and >= returns true in that case. That's undefined behavior from the algorithm's point of view, and like most undefined behavior, it doesn't fail consistently -- it only shows up with input that actually contains equal or duplicate values, which is exactly the 'only on certain inputs' pattern described here. The fix is just switching >= to >.
commonMistakes: Not knowing std::sort's comparator must satisfy strict weak ordering (comp(x,x) must be false)
Assuming any boolean-returning comparator is automatically valid as long as it compiles
Debugging the input data instead of the comparator itself, since the bug only appears with certain data
keyPoints: std::sort requires its comparator to implement strict weak ordering
A valid comparator must return false when comparing an element to an equal value
>= violates this because it returns true for equal values
Violating strict weak ordering is undefined behavior and often only surfaces with duplicate/equal input values

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies the strict-weak-ordering violation
Correctly explains why this causes undefined behavior in std::sort
Explains why the bug only appears with certain (equal-valued) input
Provides the correct fix

questions.title: Why the Pricing Core Should Never Include a pybind11 Header
questions.prompt: A capstone pricing library's design says 'the C++ pricing core never includes a pybind11 header.' Why is that specific rule worth enforcing, rather than just binding things wherever it's convenient?
questions.modelAnswer: The rule separates the project into a pure C++ core (EuropeanOption, Bond, pricing math) with no knowledge of Python at all, and a thin pybind11 bindings layer on top that's the only place translating between Python/NumPy types and the core's plain C++ types. This matters for a concrete, practical reason: it makes the pricing core independently unit-testable with a plain C++ test harness, with no Python interpreter involved anywhere in that test run -- tests run faster and have one less moving part that could mask where a bug actually lives. It also keeps the core reusable: if the library is later also needed from a C++ command-line tool, or another binding layer entirely, the core doesn't have to change at all, because it never depended on pybind11 in the first place. Mixing pybind11 calls directly into the pricing logic 'wherever convenient' would couple correctness-critical math code to a binding library's API, making both harder to test and harder to reuse.
questions.professionalAnswer: The reasoning is pretty concrete: if the core never touches pybind11, I can write and run C++ tests against the pricing logic with no Python interpreter anywhere in the loop -- faster tests, and one less place for a bug to hide. It also means the same core could be reused from a plain C++ tool or a different binding layer later without touching a single line. Scattering pybind11 calls through the actual pricing math instead would tie correctness-critical code to a specific binding library's API for no real benefit.
commonMistakes: Mixing pybind11 binding code directly into pricing logic for convenience, coupling the two unnecessarily
Assuming the separation is just a style preference rather than enabling independent, Python-free unit testing
Not recognizing that this separation also makes the core reusable from contexts other than Python

The bindings layer is a thin translation layer on top, the only place touching pybind11
This separation enables independent unit testing of the core with no Python interpreter involved
It also keeps the core reusable from other contexts (a CLI tool, a different binding layer)

questions.title: The Five Moving Parts Every Backtest Needs
questions.prompt: A junior researcher's backtest script computes a signal and prints a return number, with no mention of execution assumptions or costs. What's structurally missing from their mental model of what a backtest actually is?
questions.modelAnswer: Every backtest, no matter how simple, has five distinct moving parts: data (the historical prices feeding it), signal (the rule turning data into a view), position (the signal sized into an actual target holding), execution (the simulated act of getting from the current position to the target, at some price, with some cost, with some delay), and P&L (the resulting profit or loss accumulated over time). A script that only computes a signal and prints a return has implicitly skipped the execution step entirely -- it's very likely assuming trades fill instantly, at the exact signal price, for free, which is exactly the naive oversimplification that the apparent 'edge' of a backtest usually quietly comes from. Structurally, what's missing is any explicit model of execution: at what price does the trade actually happen, what delay is there between generating the signal and acting on it, and what transaction costs apply. Without modeling those honestly, the number being printed isn't really measuring 'how would this strategy have performed' -- it's measuring a much easier, and much less meaningful, question.
questions.professionalAnswer: What's missing is the execution and cost layer -- two of the five things every backtest actually has, alongside data, signal, and position. A script that just computes a signal and reports a return is implicitly assuming instant, free, exact-price fills, and that assumption is almost always where a chunk of a backtest's apparent edge is quietly coming from. I'd push back before trusting that number at all: what price does a trade actually fill at, how much delay is there between the signal and the trade, and what does it cost. Skip those and you're not really measuring what the strategy would have done, you're measuring something much easier and much less useful.
commonMistakes: Treating a backtest as just 'signal in, return out' without an explicit execution and cost model
Not recognizing that naive execution assumptions (instant, free, exact-price fills) are a major source of a backtest's apparent edge
Assuming a higher reported return automatically means a better, more trustworthy strategy

A naive backtest often gets execution wrong by assuming instant, free, exact-price fills
That naive execution assumption is a common hidden source of a backtest's apparent edge
A credible backtest result requires explicit, stated execution and cost assumptions

Correctly identifies execution/cost modeling as what's missing

questions.title: The Minimal Shape of an Event-Driven Backtester Loop
questions.prompt: Describe, at a structural level, what a minimal event-driven backtester needs to track and do on every single bar, using a moving-average crossover strategy as the example.
questions.modelAnswer: At minimum, an event-driven backtester needs an explicit, tracked portfolio state (cash and current share count), and on every bar in the loop it performs the same sequence: look at yesterday's completed values (not today's, to avoid look-ahead bias) to decide whether the strategy wants to be long or flat; if the desired position differs from the current one, simulate a trade at today's bar (commonly the open, not the price the decision was based on) to move from the current position toward the desired one, updating cash and shares accordingly; and finally record the portfolio's current equity (cash plus shares times today's price) into a running equity curve. The key structural discipline is that the decision at step i is based strictly on information available before bar i (typically bar i-1's completed values), and the trade executes at a bar's price that is itself not the price the decision was computed from -- the loop structure itself is what enforces no-look-ahead, rather than relying on remembering to shift a column the way a vectorized approach does.
questions.professionalAnswer: The minimum shape is: keep an explicit cash/shares state, and on each bar, decide using only data from before that bar (yesterday's moving averages, not today's), trade at today's price if the desired position differs from the current one, and record the resulting equity. The important discipline is architectural, not just a detail: the loop's structure -- decide on yesterday, trade today -- is what prevents look-ahead bias by construction, rather than relying on a programmer remembering to shift a column the way you'd have to in a vectorized version.
commonMistakes: Letting the decision on bar i use bar i's own data instead of strictly earlier data, introducing look-ahead bias
Not tracking portfolio state explicitly (cash and shares), and instead trying to infer it after the fact
Executing the simulated trade at the same price the decision was computed from, rather than a later, genuinely tradeable price
keyPoints: An event-driven backtester tracks explicit portfolio state: cash and current position
Each bar's decision uses only data available before that bar, enforced by the loop's structure
A simulated trade executes at a genuinely tradeable price, not the price the decision was based on
Equity is recorded each bar from the tracked cash/shares state, building the equity curve

Correctly describes deciding on prior-bar data to avoid look-ahead
Correctly describes trading at a later, genuinely tradeable price

questions.title: Why Use an Existing Backtesting Framework Instead of Rolling Your Own
questions.prompt: A developer argues their hand-rolled backtester is 'simpler and I understand every line,' and resists adopting a framework like backtesting.py or vectorbt. What's the actual case for the framework?
questions.modelAnswer: Understanding every line of a hand-rolled engine is genuinely valuable -- that's exactly why learning to build one by hand first is worth doing -- but it's a different question from whether production research should keep running on it. A framework exists specifically to handle the parts of a backtest that are easy to get subtly wrong and tedious to rebuild every time: applying commissions and slippage consistently to every single fill, avoiding accidental look-ahead bias in the core loop, handling different order types, and computing a standard, trustworthy set of performance statistics. Every one of those is a chance for a quiet, hard-to-notice bug in hand-rolled code, and a mature, widely-used framework has already had those bugs found and fixed by a much larger set of users than any one team's internal engine ever will. Using a framework doesn't remove the need to understand what's happening underneath, and it doesn't remove the responsibility of configuring realistic assumptions -- it just removes a large amount of error-prone boilerplate that isn't actually where the team's engineering effort should be going.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't argue against understanding the internals -- building one by hand first is exactly how you earn the right to trust a framework's defaults. But understanding every line of your own engine and continuing to maintain it in production are two different costs. A framework has already had its commission/slippage/look-ahead-bias edge cases found and fixed by far more users than any one team will ever generate internally. The responsibility for configuring realistic assumptions doesn't go away, but a huge amount of error-prone boilerplate does, and that's time better spent on the actual research.

questions.title: Why Price-Adjustment Logic Shouldn't Live Inside the Signal Code
questions.prompt: A strategy's signal code directly reads a raw price CSV and computes its own split adjustment inline, mixed in with the actual trading logic. Why is that a design problem, independent of whether the adjustment math is correct?
questions.modelAnswer: Mixing data-cleaning concerns (split/dividend adjustment, gap handling, timezone normalization) directly into the signal logic couples two things that should be independent: whether the trading rule is correct, and whether the data feeding it is correct. If a split-adjustment bug is ever found, it has to be hunted down and fixed inside every single strategy that happened to inline its own copy of that logic, instead of in one place. It also makes the signal code harder to reason about and test in isolation -- a unit test for 'does this crossover rule work correctly' now has to also account for 'and does the inline adjustment logic also behave correctly on this test data,' conflating two separate questions. The better design is a dedicated data-handling layer that produces already-adjusted, already-cleaned data, with the signal code consuming that clean data and focusing purely on the trading rule itself -- the same separation-of-concerns argument that applies to keeping an OMS layer separate from strategy logic on the execution side.
questions.professionalAnswer: The problem isn't whether the adjustment math is right today -- it's that two genuinely separate concerns, data correctness and trading-rule correctness, are now tangled together in one place. If a split-adjustment bug shows up later, you're hunting through every strategy that inlined its own copy instead of fixing it once. It also makes testing harder, since a test of the trading rule now implicitly depends on the adjustment logic behaving correctly too. I'd want a dedicated data layer that hands the signal code already-clean, already-adjusted data, so the signal code's only job is the actual trading rule.

Not recognizing that a future adjustment bug would then need fixing in every strategy separately
Missing that mixing concerns also makes the signal logic harder to test in isolation

Separating data handling makes signal logic easier to test and reason about in isolation

questions.title: Why Paper Trading Exists as a Separate Stage
questions.prompt: A strategy already passed a careful, realistic backtest. Why is paper trading still a required stage before risking real capital, rather than a redundant extra step?
questions.modelAnswer: A backtest, no matter how realistic, runs entirely against data the researcher already has in full, through code that's typically run once, offline. Paper trading exercises something a backtest structurally cannot: the actual live pipeline, running continuously, unattended, against data arriving in real time -- does the live data feed actually arrive in the format the signal code expects, does the order-generation logic run fast enough and reliably enough bar after bar without a human babysitting it, and does the strategy behave sanely around real-world glitches like a stale quote or a halted symbol that clean historical data never has. These are infrastructure and operational risks, not strategy-logic risks, and a backtest's realism, however careful, can never rehearse them because a backtest was never actually running the live pipeline in the first place. Paper trading is the stage that specifically tests whether the strategy's code can survive contact with the operational reality it will actually run in.
questions.professionalAnswer: A backtest, even a careful one, is still running offline against data you already have in full -- it never actually exercises the live pipeline. Paper trading is the stage that does: does the real-time data feed show up the way the signal code expects, does order generation keep running reliably without someone watching it, does the strategy handle a stale quote or a halted symbol the way clean historical data never forced it to. None of that is about whether the trading logic itself is sound -- it's about whether the actual running system survives contact with live, messy, real-time reality, which no amount of backtest realism can rehearse.
commonMistakes: Treating paper trading as redundant once a backtest is realistic, rather than testing a different category of risk

Assuming a backtest's realistic cost modeling is a substitute for actually running the live pipeline

questions.title: Why Use a Template Instead of Three Copy-Pasted Functions
questions.prompt: A codebase has weightedAverageDouble, weightedAverageInt, and weightedAverageDecimal, three near-identical copy-pasted functions differing only in their argument type. What's the architectural case for replacing them with a single template?
questions.modelAnswer: A function template lets you write the weighted-average logic exactly once, parameterized over a type T, and the compiler generates a correct, type-specific version for every type it's actually called with -- with zero runtime dispatch cost, since each instantiation is just an ordinary, separately compiled function under the hood. The copy-pasted three-function version has a maintenance problem baked in: if a bug is found or the formula needs to change, it has to be fixed in three separate places, and it's entirely possible for the copies to quietly drift out of sync with each other over time as one gets updated and the others don't. The template version has exactly one implementation to maintain, and adding support for a fourth numeric type later costs nothing beyond calling the template with that type -- no new function to write at all. The only real cost is that each distinct set of template arguments generates its own compiled code, which can modestly increase binary size if many very different types are actually instantiated -- a cost worth knowing about but rarely significant in practice for something like this.
questions.professionalAnswer: The problem with the three-function version isn't that it's wrong today, it's that it's three separate places for the same logic to quietly drift apart over time. A template collapses that to one implementation -- the compiler generates a correct version per type you actually call it with, at zero runtime cost, and adding a fourth type later is free, no new function needed. The only real tradeoff is a bit of extra compiled code size per distinct type actually instantiated, which almost never matters in practice for something this small.
commonMistakes: Underestimating the maintenance risk of copy-pasted near-duplicate functions drifting apart over time
Assuming templates add a runtime performance cost compared to the hand-written duplicated functions
Not mentioning that each template instantiation does generate its own separately compiled code (a minor, usually acceptable cost)
keyPoints: A function template expresses the logic once, with the compiler generating a type-specific version per call
Templates have zero runtime dispatch cost compared to the hand-duplicated versions
Copy-pasted near-duplicate functions risk drifting out of sync as one is updated and others aren't
Templates increase compiled code size per distinct instantiated type, a usually-acceptable tradeoff

Explains the maintenance risk of duplicated code the template avoids
Mentions the zero-runtime-cost property and the binary-size tradeoff

questions.title: std::optional vs. a Sentinel Value for 'No Price Available'
questions.prompt: A lookupPrice function currently returns -1.0 to mean 'no price available for this symbol.' What's architecturally wrong with that design, and how does std::optional<double> fix it?
questions.modelAnswer: A sentinel value like -1.0 overloads a single double to mean two completely different things -- a real, negative price (which can genuinely occur for certain instruments, like negative interest rates or spreads) and 'no value at all' -- with nothing in the function's type signature telling a caller this ambiguity exists. A caller who forgets to check for -1.0 specifically will silently treat it as a real price and proceed with obviously wrong downstream math, and the compiler has no way to catch that mistake, because as far as the type system is concerned, -1.0 is just an ordinary double. std::optional<double> fixes this by making 'might not have a value' part of the type itself: the function returns std::optional<double>, callers must explicitly check whether a value is present (if (auto px = lookupPrice(...))) before extracting it, and there's no numeric value left over that could collide with a genuinely valid price. The absence of a value becomes a distinct, type-level state instead of a magic number a caller has to remember to special-case.
questions.professionalAnswer: The problem with -1.0 as a sentinel is that it's overloading one double to mean two different things, and nothing in the type system flags that ambiguity -- a caller who forgets to check for it just silently treats -1.0 as a real price and keeps going. std::optional<double> fixes that structurally: 'no value' becomes a real, distinct state in the type itself, the caller is forced to check presence before extracting the value, and there's no leftover numeric value that could ever collide with a genuinely valid (even negative) price.
commonMistakes: Not recognizing that a sentinel value can collide with a genuinely valid value (e.g. a real negative price)
Assuming the compiler would catch a caller forgetting to check for the sentinel value
Treating std::optional as just a style preference rather than a type-safety improvement
keyPoints: A sentinel value overloads one type to mean both 'a real value' and 'no value,' ambiguously
The compiler cannot catch a caller forgetting to check for a sentinel value
std::optional<T> makes 'might not have a value' part of the type itself
Callers must explicitly check presence before extracting the value from an optional

questions.title: Evaluating Your First Quant Developer Offer
questions.prompt: You've received your first real offer as a quant developer, with a base salary and a bonus structure you don't fully understand yet. How should you approach evaluating it before accepting?
questions.modelAnswer: The first step is understanding that quant compensation structures vary significantly by firm type -- a systematic hedge fund, a prop trading firm, a bank's quant desk, and a fintech company each weight base salary, bonus, and profit-share very differently, so the same headline base number can represent very different total compensation and very different year-to-year variance depending on which type of firm is offering it. Before reacting to the number itself, it's worth understanding exactly how the bonus is determined -- team performance, individual contribution, desk PnL, or fully discretionary -- since a profit-share-heavy structure can pay far more in a good year and far less in a bad one than a steadier structure with the same headline base. It's also worth building a quick researched range from at least two independent sources (aggregated salary sites read skeptically, actual live postings for comparable roles at comparable firm types, and your own network) before deciding whether the offer is fair, rather than evaluating it purely against gut feeling. Beyond the number, weigh mentorship opportunities, the firm's actual risk and research culture, and what the role concretely does day to day -- a 'quant developer' title can mean very different things at different firms.
questions.professionalAnswer: First thing I'd do is figure out what kind of firm this actually is, because compensation structure varies by firm type more than by title -- a bank desk, a prop shop, and a systematic fund can all offer the same base number with wildly different bonus mechanics and variance behind it. I'd ask directly how the bonus is actually determined before assuming anything. I'd also build a quick researched range from a couple of independent sources rather than just trusting my gut on whether the number is fair. And I'd weigh the non-number stuff seriously -- mentorship, the firm's actual research/risk culture, what the role does day to day -- since those tend to matter more to how the next few years actually go than a modest difference in the base number.

Not researching comparable compensation at comparable firm types before judging whether the offer is fair
Ignoring non-compensation factors like mentorship, culture fit, and actual day-to-day role content

Understand exactly how the bonus is determined before judging the offer
Build a researched range from independent sources before deciding if a number is fair
Weigh mentorship, culture, and actual day-to-day role content alongside the compensation number
